%% ==== file: main.tex ====
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We construct a total Boolean function $f$ for which $\operatorname{Q}(f) = \widetilde{O}(\sqrt[4]{\operatorname{C}(f)})$, where $\operatorname{Q}(f)$ denotes the bounded-error quantum query complexity and $\operatorname{C}(f)$ denotes the certificate complexity. This resolves a longstanding open question and is
tight up to logarithmic factors.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
We determine, up to polylogarithmic factors, how large certificate complexity can be relative to bounded-error quantum query complexity for a total Boolean function.

Certificate complexity $\operatorname{C}(f)$ 
is one of the most fundamental combinatorial complexity measures for Boolean functions (along with the block sensitivity and polynomial
degree of a function). $\operatorname{C}(f)$ is tightly connected to query complexity of $f$ in deterministic, randomized and quantum models of computation.
Let $\operatorname{D}(f), \operatorname{R}(f)$ and $\operatorname{Q}(f)$ denote these three complexity measures (with bounded error in the latter two cases).
For total Boolean functions $f$, we have $\operatorname{C}(f) \leq \operatorname{D}(f) \leq \operatorname{C}(f)^2$ \cite{Tardos1989}, $\operatorname{R}(f) = \Omega(\sqrt{\operatorname{C}(f)})$ and $\operatorname{R}(f) \leq \operatorname{C}(f)^2$ \cite{Nisan1991}, and $\operatorname{Q}(f) = \Omega(\sqrt[4]{\operatorname{C}(f)})$ and $\operatorname{Q}(f) \leq \operatorname{C}(f)^2$ \cite{Beals2001}. In particular, this implies that deterministic, randomized and quantum complexities are all polynomially related. 

Moreover, some of the bounds relating $\operatorname{Q}(f)$, $\operatorname{R}(f)$ and $\operatorname{D}(f)$ use certificate complexity as an intermediate quantity in the proof.
For example, $\operatorname{D}(f) = O(\operatorname{R}(f)^3)$ \cite{Nisan1991} which is currently the best relation between $\operatorname{R}(f)$ and $\operatorname{D}(f)$ uses $\operatorname{C}(f)$ as an intermediate quantity.
Also, $\operatorname{D}(f) = O(\operatorname{Q}(f)^6)$ by Beals et al. \cite{Beals2001} (which was the best result for a long time) uses $\operatorname{C}(f)$ although the more recent relation $\operatorname{D}(f) = O(\operatorname{Q}(f)^4)$ \cite{Aaronson2021} does not use it.

Given the fundamental nature of $\operatorname{C}(f)$ and its close relationship to query complexity measures, it is interesting to settle the question about maximum possible
gap between $\operatorname{C}(f)$ and $\operatorname{Q}(f)$. The research in the last decade \cite{Aaronson2021,cornelissen} has settled many of the other gaps between query and combinatorial complexity measures for total Boolean functions but this gap remains open.

In the direction considered in this paper, the OR function gives
\[
\operatorname{C}(f)=\Theta(\operatorname{Q}(f)^2),
\]
and no larger separation was previously known. On the other hand, the general bound $\operatorname{C}(f)=O(\operatorname{Q}(f)^4)$ \cite{Aaronson2021} leaves open the possibility of a quartic separation. Thus the optimal exponent relating $\operatorname{C}(f)$ to $\operatorname{Q}(f)$ was known only to lie between 2 and 4.

In this paper, we close the gap (up to polylogarithmic factors), by constructing a function $f$ for which $\operatorname{Q}(f) = \widetilde{O}(\sqrt[4]{\operatorname{C}(f)})$.
Our construction builds on the work of Pabbaraju \cite{pabbaraju2026} who constructed a family of total Boolean functions satisfying $\operatorname{C}(f) = \widetilde{\Omega}(\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)^4)$. Here, $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)$ is the least degree of a real polynomial that approximates $f$ with error at most $1 / 3$ on every input. It is known that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f) \leq 2\operatorname{Q}(f)$ \cite{Beals2001}
but $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)$ can be asymptotically smaller than $\operatorname{Q}(f)$.
Therefore, establishing the corresponding quantum separation requires an upper bound on quantum query complexity.

\cite{pabbaraju2026} uses a partial function whose domain is specified by a disjunctive normal form (DNF) with mutually incompatible conjunctions of input literals. A satisfied conjunction identifies a block and a set of positions within it; the partial function returns the OR of additional input bits at those positions. The cheat-sheet construction \cite{AaronsonBenDavidKothari2016} totalizes this partial function using an array of certificate descriptions; at most one cell is valid, and the total function is one if and only if such a cell exists. \cite{pabbaraju2026} obtains the approximate degree upper bound by summing polynomials that approximate the individual cell tests.

We also use the cheat-sheet totalization of the partial function and retain the way the partial function is constructed from the underlying DNF, while modifying how the DNF is defined to obtain a slightly different total Boolean function. On positive inputs, our quantum algorithm first computes the values determining the cell address and then verifies the addressed cell. Computing each value requires locating the block identified by the satisfied conjunction. We locate this block by finding a source in a directed complete graph defined by comparisons between blocks. The algorithm adapts the variable-time search construction of \cite{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs}; its query bound follows from estimates for the successive candidate sets and the query counts of their membership tests.

\section{Result and proof outline}

For a positive integer $m$, write $[m] = \{1,\ldots,m\}$, and put $[0] = \emptyset$.  For a total Boolean function $f : \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}$, let $\operatorname{Q}(f)$ denote bounded-error quantum query complexity and let $\operatorname{C}(f)$ denote certificate complexity.  For $b \in \{0,1\}$ and $x \in f^{-1}(b)$, write $\operatorname{C}_b(f,x)$ for the size of a smallest $b$-certificate for $x$.

The relations in \cite[Section~2.3]{AaronsonBenDavidKothari2016} imply the bound $\operatorname{C}(f) = O(\operatorname{Q}(f)^4)$. We show that the exponent four is attained up to logarithmic factors. Independent proofs of the analogous separation between certificate complexity and approximate degree appear in \cite[Theorem~4]{pabbaraju2026} and \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Balodis}.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
For all sufficiently large $n$, there is a total Boolean function $F_n$ on $\Theta(n^3 \ln^2 n)$ bits such that
\[
 \operatorname{C}(F_n) \geq n \left(\left\lceil \frac{n}{2}\right\rceil + 1\right) = \Omega(n^2),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Q}(F_n) = O\left(\sqrt{n} \ln^3 n\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

The two bounds in \Cref{thm:main} follow from \Cref{lem:certificate-lower,lem:query-transfer,lem:query-upper}.

A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is a disjunction of terms, each a conjunction of variables or their negations. It is \emph{unambiguous} if every input satisfies at most one term.

We adapt the construction of \cite[Section~3]{pabbaraju2026}, replacing its bijections associated with pairs of blocks by fixed position lists. The resulting DNF is unambiguous, and the $O(n)$ bound on the total prefix length gives $O(n)$ literals per term. When $x$ satisfies its unique term $(i,S)$, the partial function $H$ returns $\bigvee_{p \in S} y_i(p)$. Its value can be certified by a description with $O(n)$ checks, and the standard cheat-sheet construction totalizes $H$. At the all-zero input, every partial assignment of size below $n \left(\lceil n / 2 \rceil + 1\right)$ leaves a cheat-sheet cell with no fixed coordinate and permits every input to $H$ to be completed to either value.

To evaluate $H$, the algorithm finds the block of the satisfied term and then applies Grover search within that block. The position lists and the input define a directed complete graph whose source is that block. To ensure that the bound on total prefix length applies whenever the algorithm compares two blocks, we modify the edge directions using the outcomes of a test based on random positions. With probability at least $11 / 12$, the modified graph has the same source and every block that passes the test has more than $n / 3$ ones. The procedure $\mathrm{FindSource}$ stores an ordered list $W$ and searches the candidate set $U(W)$ of vertices outside $W$ that point to every vertex in $W$. Bounds on the sizes of these candidate sets and on the squared stopping query counts of their membership tests give an $O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$-query algorithm for $H$. \Cref{sec:source-proof} proves this bound from the search and candidate estimates, then applies robust address recovery and cell verification to evaluate $F_n$. The supporting constructions and proofs follow in the appendices.

\section{Construction and basic bounds}

This section adapts the construction and certificate arguments of \cite[Sections~3 and~5]{pabbaraju2026} to the position lists and description format used here. We prove \Cref{lem:first-hit-sum} below; the remaining proofs are straightforward and given in \Cref{app:construction}.

\subsection{Position lists}

The position lists determine the prefixes used in the DNF and in the comparisons between blocks.

Fix $n \geq 6$.  Put $k = \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor$, $M = 8 n$, and $\tau_n = n (\lceil n / 2 \rceil + 1)$.  Write each $x, y \in \{0,1\}^{n^2}$ as $n$ blocks of length $n$, with $x_i(p)$ and $y_i(p)$ denoting the bits at position $p$ in block $i$.  For each $j \in [n]$, let $P_j \in [n]^M$ be a list, with repetitions allowed, and write $P_j(a)$ for its $a$th entry.  For $S \subseteq [n]$, define $m_j(S) = \min\{a \in [M] : P_j(a) \in S\}$ when this set is nonempty, and define $m_j(S) = M + 1$ otherwise.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:first-hit-sum}
The lists $P_1, \ldots, P_n$ can be chosen so that every $S \subseteq [n]$ with $|S| \geq n / 3$ satisfies
\[
 \sum_{j = 1}^n m_j(S) \leq 8 n.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose all list entries independently and uniformly from $[n]$, and fix $S$ with $|S| \geq n / 3$. For the analysis, extend each list to an infinite sequence by choosing further entries independently and uniformly from $[n]$. For a fixed $j$, the first entry in the extension of $P_j$ that lies in $S$ occurs at index $a \geq 1$ with probability $(|S| / n)(1 - |S| / n)^{a - 1}$: the first $a - 1$ entries lie outside $S$, and the $a$th entry lies in $S$. If $a \leq M$, then $m_j(S) = a$; if $a > M$, then $m_j(S) = M + 1 \leq a$. Hence
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^{m_j(S)}\right]
 \leq \sum_{a = 1}^{\infty} \frac{|S|}{n} \left(1 - \frac{|S|}{n}\right)^{a - 1} \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^a
 = \frac{5 |S|}{5 |S| - n} \leq \frac{5}{2}.
\]
Independence gives $\mathbb E[(5 / 4)^{\sum_{j = 1}^n m_j(S)}] \leq (5 / 2)^n$.  Markov's inequality therefore gives
\[
 \Pr\left[\sum_{j = 1}^n m_j(S) > 8 n\right] \leq \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^n \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{8 n}.
\]

There are fewer than $2^n$ sets $S \subseteq [n]$ with $|S| \geq n / 3$.  A union bound therefore shows that the probability that some such set satisfies $\sum_{j = 1}^n m_j(S) > 8 n$ is less than $2^n (5 / 2)^n (4 / 5)^{8 n} = [5 (4 / 5)^8]^n < 1$.  Hence there exists a family of lists satisfying $\sum_{j = 1}^n m_j(S) \leq 8 n$ for every $S \subseteq [n]$ with $|S| \geq n / 3$.  Every list in this family intersects every such set, since one value $m_j(S) = M + 1$ would make the sum exceed $8 n$.
\end{proof}

Fix any family satisfying \Cref{lem:first-hit-sum}.  For distinct $i,j$ and $|S| \geq n / 3$, define the prefix set
\[
 A_{ij}(S) = \{P_i(a) : 1 \leq a \leq m_j(S)\}.
\]
Thus $P_j$ determines the prefix length $m_j(S)$. The set $A_{ij}(S)$ consists of the distinct entries among $P_i(1),\ldots,P_i(m_j(S))$, so $|A_{ij}(S)| \leq m_j(S)$.

This adapts the construction of \cite[Section~3]{pabbaraju2026}. There, for every ordered pair $(i,j)$ with $i \neq j$, a bijection from block $i$ to $[n]$ is fixed, and $m_{i,j}(S)$ is the minimum value of this bijection on $S$. Here $P_j$ is independent of $i$ and defines $m_j(S)$ as the least index $a$ such that $P_j(a) \in S$. \cite[Section~3]{pabbaraju2026} chooses the bijections so that $\sum_{j \neq i} m_{i,j}(S) = O(n)$ for every term $(i,S)$. \Cref{lem:first-hit-sum} holds simultaneously for every $S$ of size at least $n / 3$, as required by the quantum query bound.

\subsection{The DNF and the partial function}

We use the prefix sets to define terms whose positive literals lie in one block.

For $i \in [n]$ and $S \subseteq [n]$ with $|S| = k$, the term $(i,S)$ requires $x_i(p) = 1$ for every $p \in S$ and $x_i(p) = 0$ for every $p \in [n] \setminus S$. It also requires $x_j(p) = 0$ for every $j \neq i$ and $p \in A_{ij}(S)$.  Define
\[
 f(x) = \bigvee_{i \in [n]}\ \bigvee_{\substack{S \subseteq [n]\\ |S| = k}}
 \left(\bigwedge_{p \in S} x_i(p)\right)
 \left(\bigwedge_{p \in [n] \setminus S} \neg x_i(p)\right)
 \left(\bigwedge_{j \neq i}\ \bigwedge_{p \in A_{ij}(S)} \neg x_j(p)\right).
\]
This follows the DNF construction of \cite[Section~3]{pabbaraju2026}, replacing the prefix sets defined by its bijections with the sets $A_{ij}(S)$ defined from the position lists.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:dnf-unambiguous}
The DNF $f$ is unambiguous.
\end{lemma}

When $x$ satisfies the term $(i,S)$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:partial-function}
 H(x,y) = \bigvee_{p \in S} y_i(p).
\end{equation}
Set $H(x,y) = *$ when $f(x) = 0$, so the domain of $H$ consists of the pairs $(x,y)$ with $f(x) = 1$.  We define $H$ from the DNF $f$ as in \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026}, except that here the position lists, rather than the bijections associated with pairs of blocks, determine $f$. If $(i,S)$ is the unique term satisfied by $x$, then $H(x,y)$ is the OR of the $y$-bits indexed by $S$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:undefined-input}
At the all-zero input, $H$ is undefined.  Every partial assignment consistent with this input and fixing fewer than $\tau_n$ coordinates has completions in the domain of $H$ on which $H$ equals zero and one, respectively.
\end{lemma}

\subsection{Cheat-sheet totalization}

We adapt the certificate descriptions of \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026} to verify $H(x,y) = \beta$. The checks verify that a term $(i,S)$ is satisfied and that $\bigvee_{p \in S} y_i(p) = \beta$.

The fields allow the $O(n)$ checks to be indexed in advance, with each check reading $O(1)$ fields and $O(1)$ bits of $(x,y)$.

A \emph{description} is a tuple
\[
 (i,w_1,\ldots,w_n,\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n,j_1,\ldots,j_M,p^\star),
\]
where $i \in [n]$, every $w_p,j_t,p^\star \in \{0,\ldots,n\}$, and every $\sigma_j \in \{0,\ldots,M\}$.  The fields $i,w_p,j_t,p^\star$ each use $\lceil \log_2(n + 1) \rceil$ bits, and each $\sigma_j$ uses $\lceil \log_2(M + 1) \rceil$ bits.  The description thus has $\Theta(n \ln n)$ bits.

On input $(x,y)$, the description is \emph{accepted} for $\beta$ when the following four groups of checks pass:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Count checks.} With $w_0 = 0$, these checks require $w_n = k$ and $w_p = w_{p - 1} + x_i(p)$ for every $p \in [n]$. Thus $w_p$ counts the ones in the first $p$ positions of block $i$, and $S = \{p : x_i(p) = 1\}$ has cardinality $k$. These counts replace the stored list of positions in $S$ in \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026}.

\item\label{cond:description-lengths} \textbf{Length checks.} With $\sigma_0 = 0$ and $\ell_j = \sigma_j - \sigma_{j - 1}$ for $j \in [n]$, these checks require $\ell_i = 0$, and require $\ell_j \geq 1$ and $x_i(P_j(\ell_j)) = 1$ for every $j \neq i$. The field $\sigma_j$ is the cumulative prefix length through block $j$, omitting block $i$. For $j \neq i$, the condition $x_i(P_j(\ell_j)) = 1$ implies $m_j(S) \leq \ell_j$. The zero checks in block $j$ use positions $P_i(1),\ldots,P_i(\ell_j)$. This replaces the separate fields in \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026} for an element of $S$ and its image under the bijection defining $m_{i,j}(S)$.

\item \textbf{Zero checks.} The zero checks are numbered consecutively in increasing block order, so the zero checks for block $j$ have indices $\sigma_{j - 1} + 1,\ldots,\sigma_j$. For $t \in [M]$ with $t > \sigma_n$, the check requires $j_t = 0$. Otherwise it takes $j = j_t$, requires $j \in [n]$ and $\sigma_{j - 1} < t \leq \sigma_j$, sets $a = t - \sigma_{j - 1}$, and checks $x_j(P_i(a)) = 0$. For $t \leq \sigma_n$, the field $j_t$ specifies the block checked at index $t$, and the cumulative lengths determine the prefix position $a$.

\item \textbf{Value checks.} For $\beta = 0$, the checks require $p^\star = 0$ and, for every $p \in [n]$, require $y_i(p) = 0$ whenever $x_i(p) = 1$. For $\beta = 1$, they require $p^\star \in [n]$ and $x_i(p^\star) = y_i(p^\star) = 1$, so $p^\star$ specifies a position in block $i$; \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026} instead stores an index in the list of positions in $S$.
\end{enumerate}

The integers in the specified ranges have fixed binary encodings, and every other codeword is rejected.  Before using an encoded or derived value as an index, each check verifies that it lies in the set being indexed and rejects otherwise.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:description-verification}
If a description is accepted for $\beta$, then $H(x,y) = \beta$. Conversely, every input in the domain of $H$ has an accepted description for its value. Acceptance is the conjunction of $O(n)$ checks, each evaluated deterministically with $O(\ln n)$ queries.
\end{lemma}

Put $r = \lfloor \log_2 \tau_n \rfloor + 1$. Apply the standard cheat-sheet construction of \cite{AaronsonBenDavidKothari2016}, in the form used for $G$ in \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026}, to $r$ disjoint inputs to $H$.  An input to $F_n$ contains these inputs and a cheat-sheet array with one cell for each $a \in \{0,1\}^r$.  Cell $a = (a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ contains one description for each input to $H$ and accepts when its $\ell$th description is accepted for $\beta = a_\ell$ on the $\ell$th input for every $\ell \in [r]$.  Define $F_n = 1$ if and only if some cell accepts.

The position lists and the description format make $F_n$ a slightly different total Boolean function from $G$ in \cite[Section~5]{pabbaraju2026}. Invalid field encodings are rejected, so every cell either accepts or rejects on every input and $F_n$ is total. By \Cref{lem:description-verification}, every cell rejects if one input to $H$ lies outside its domain; otherwise only the cell addressed by the string of $H$-values can accept.

Since $\tau_n < 2^r \leq 2 \tau_n$, the cheat-sheet array contains $2^r r$ descriptions of $\Theta(n \ln n)$ bits, giving $\Theta(n^3 \ln^2 n)$ bits in total.  The $r$ inputs to $H$ have $2 r n^2 = O(n^2 \ln n)$ bits.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:certificate-lower}
The all-zero input $Z_0$ to $F_n$ satisfies $\operatorname{C}_0(F_n,Z_0) = \tau_n$.
\end{lemma}

\section{Quantum query upper bound}\label{sec:source-proof}

On inputs in the domain of $H$, the algorithm first finds the block of the satisfied term and then applies Grover search within that block. For distinct blocks $i,j$, let $m_{ij}$ be the first index of $P_j$ naming a one in block $i$, or $M + 1$ if there is none. As in the incompatibility argument of \cite[Section~3]{pabbaraju2026}, we compare $m_{ij}$ with $m_{ji}$. These comparisons define a directed complete graph on the $n$ blocks. The block of the satisfied term is its source. A table of random positions is first chosen for all blocks. The bits at a block's chosen positions are queried only when its classification is needed. With probability at least $11 / 12$, the block of the satisfied term passes the test and every block of Hamming weight at most $n / 3$ fails it. First indices are then compared only between two passing blocks; the remaining directions are determined by the test results and the block indices, preserving the source.

The procedure $\mathrm{FindSource}$ described in \Cref{subsec:source-algorithm} starts with one uniformly selected vertex and searches for a vertex pointing to all vertices already selected. Each returned vertex is appended to the list. When a search returns $\bot$, the procedure returns the last selected vertex. The analysis combines variable-time search with bounds on the number and sizes of the candidate sets and on the sum of squared query counts for their membership tests. These estimates give the following lemma.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:block-finding}
For all sufficiently large $n$, if $x$ satisfies the term $(i,S)$, then $\mathrm{FindSource}$ returns the block index $i$ with probability at least $5 / 6$, where the probability is over the random positions and the measurement outcomes of the procedure. Its output lies in $[n]$ on every input. The unitary circuit constructed in \Cref{app:source-implementation} has a fixed query count $O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$ on every input; measuring its output register gives the output distribution of $\mathrm{FindSource}$.
\end{lemma}

The proof is given in \Cref{subsec:source-algorithm}, after the graph and search interfaces have been introduced.
The following reduction then gives the query bound for $F_n$.
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:query-transfer}
Suppose an algorithm for $H$ has error at most $1 / 4$ on its domain and has a unitary implementation making exactly $T_H$ queries on every input. Then
\[
 \operatorname{Q}(F_n) = O\left(r T_H + \sqrt{n r} \ln n\right).
\]
\end{lemma}

When the $r$ inputs lie in the domain of $H$, the recovery algorithm of \cite[Theorem~3]{BuhrmanNewmanRohrigDeWolf} recovers the address using the circuit for $H$ and its inverse $O(r)$ times. The addressed cell has $O(n r)$ checks of $O(\ln n)$ queries each, so searching for a rejected check gives the second term. The proof of \Cref{lem:query-transfer} is given in \Cref{app:query-transfer}.

\subsection{Graph and candidate sets}\label{sec:graph-candidates}\label{subsec:block-graph}\label{subsec:candidate-sets}

The graph is defined so that the zeros imposed on the other blocks by a satisfied term make the term's block a source.

Fix $x \in \{0,1\}^{n^2}$ and put $S_i = \{p \in [n] : x_i(p) = 1\}$. For $i \neq j$, one has $m_{ij} = m_j(S_i)$; put $\Delta_{ij} = \min\{m_{ij}, m_{ji}\}$. If $x$ satisfies $(i,S)$, then $S_i = S$ and $m_{ij} = m_j(S)$. Direct the edge according to $m_{ij}$ and $m_{ji}$, breaking ties in favour of the smaller block index:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-direction}
 i \to j
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 m_{ij} < m_{ji}
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \bigl(m_{ij} = m_{ji} \text{ and } i < j\bigr).
\end{equation}
If $x$ satisfies $(i,S)$, then $x_j(P_i(a)) = 0$ for every $j \neq i$ and $1 \leq a \leq m_j(S)$. Hence $m_{ji} > m_j(S) = m_{ij}$ for every $j \neq i$, so $i$ is the unique source.

\paragraph{Classification test.}
The bound in \Cref{lem:first-hit-sum} applies to blocks with at least $n / 3$ ones. To use it throughout the algorithm, put $s_n = \lceil 288 \ln(12 n) \rceil$ and choose $s_n$ positions in each block independently and uniformly with replacement. The table of positions is fixed throughout $\mathrm{FindSource}$. A block is declared dense if at least $3s_n / 8$ of its bits at these positions are one, and declared sparse otherwise. Its classification is computed when needed, using $s_n$ queries; write $\gamma_i = 1$ for a block declared dense and $\gamma_i = 0$ otherwise.

The test succeeds when every block with $k$ ones is declared dense and every block declared dense has more than $n / 3$ ones. Its success probability is at least $11 / 12$ for every fixed $x$, as proved in \Cref{app:block-classification}. Let $\mathcal G$ use \eqref{eq:block-direction} between two blocks declared dense, direct every edge from a block declared dense to one declared sparse, and use the index rule between two blocks declared sparse. If $x$ satisfies $(i,S)$ and the test succeeds, then $i$ is declared dense and all its edges in $\mathcal G$ point outward. Thus $i$ is the source of $\mathcal G$.

\paragraph{Query counts for block comparisons.}
Choose an absolute constant $c_0$ so that the search circuit in \Cref{sec:edge-proof} uses at most $\lceil c_0 \sqrt{L \ln n}\rceil$ queries to $x$ on each prefix of length $L \in [M]$. Such a constant exists by \Cref{lem:prefix-search} and the simulation using four queries to $x$ per query to the comparison string. Put $\theta_{ij} = 0$ if $i = j$ or either $\gamma_i$ or $\gamma_j$ is zero; otherwise put
\[
 \theta_{ij} = \left\lceil c_0 \sqrt{\Delta_{ij} \ln n}\right\rceil.
\]
With the classifications available, equality and directions involving a block declared sparse require no queries. For two blocks declared dense, the construction in \Cref{sec:edge-proof} uses $O(\theta_{ij})$ queries to determine their direction when all comparison answers are correct.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:edge-profile}
The parameters satisfy $\theta_{ij} \geq 0$ and $\theta_{ij} = \theta_{ji}$ for all $i,j \in [n]$, and $\max_{i,j} \theta_{ij} = O(\sqrt{n \ln n})$. There is an absolute constant $K_\theta > 0$ such that, whenever the test based on the random positions succeeds,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:edge-square-sum}
 \max_i \sum_{j = 1}^n \theta_{ij}^2 \leq K_\theta n \ln n.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

The proof in \Cref{sec:edge-proof} applies \Cref{lem:first-hit-sum} to each block declared dense.

\paragraph{Candidate sets.}
The algorithm searches among vertices that point to every previously selected vertex. For an ordered list $W = (w_1,\ldots,w_h)$ of distinct vertices of $\mathcal G$, define the candidate set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:candidate-set}
 U(W) = \{v \in [n] \setminus W : v \to w \text{ for every } w \in W\},
 \qquad U(\emptyset) = [n].
\end{equation}
If $v \in U(W)$ and $W' = (w_1,\ldots,w_h,v)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:candidate-update}
 U(W') = \{u \in U(W) : u \to v\} \subseteq U(W) \setminus \{v\}.
\end{equation}
If $s$ is a source, it belongs to $U(W)$ until it is appended to $W$. Once appended, no vertex points to it, so the next candidate set is empty. Therefore repeatedly selecting a vertex from $U(W)$, appending it to $W$, and returning the last appended vertex when the updated candidate set is empty returns $s$.

A search in $U(W)$ uses a membership test that classifies $v$ once and compares it with the stored vertices in order, stopping when it finds $v = w_d$ or $w_d \to v$. For two blocks declared dense, it compares $m_{v w_d}$ with $m_{w_d v}$ by searching successively doubled prefixes, ending at length $M$. With correct comparison answers, let the stopping query count $t_v(W)$ be the sum of the query counts of the implemented circuits until the membership test returns zero or one. For a fixed input and table, these are deterministic counts. The construction in \Cref{subsec:membership} proves the following bounds.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:membership-counts}
For every input and table of positions, one has $t_v(\emptyset) = s_n$ for every $v \in [n]$. Let $W = (w_1,\ldots,w_h)$ be an ordered list of distinct vertices, let $w \in U(W)$, and put $W' = (w_1,\ldots,w_h,w)$. Then, for every $v \in [n]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:membership-completion-update}
 t_v(W') \geq t_v(W) \quad\text{and}\quad t_v(W') - t_v(W) = O(\theta_{vw}).
\end{equation}
The difference is zero for $v \notin U(W)$ and for $v = w$.
\end{lemma}

For each integer $q \geq 0$, the checking circuit $\mathcal M_q$ acts on the list register, the register holding the tested vertex, and the response register. On a basis state where the list register encodes $W$ and the tested vertex is $v$, it reports $*$ when $q < t_v(W)$ and otherwise reports the membership bit of $v$ in $U(W)$. It preserves the list and tested vertex and adds the encoded answer to the response register. We count $2 q$ queries for each application of $\mathcal M_q$ or its inverse, matching the query count of its approximate implementation $\widetilde{\mathcal M}_q$ constructed in \Cref{subsec:membership}.

For fixed $W$, the circuits $\mathcal M_q$ preserve the subspace in which the list register encodes $W$. Restricted to this subspace, they have the checking form of \cite[Section~2]{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs}, with $G = U(W)$ and $t_v = t_v(W)$. More generally, $\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2)$ is defined for any set $G \subseteq [n]$ with fixed, possibly unknown stopping query counts $t_v \geq 1$. It combines searches with different numbers of stages, following \cite[Algorithms~1 and~2]{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs}. The construction and proof of the following lemma are given in \Cref{app:variable-search}.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:full-search}
For $T_2 \geq \sqrt{n}$, every index returned by $\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2)$ belongs to $G$. Its maximum query count is $O(T_2 \ln n)$, and it returns $\bot$ with certainty when $G$ is empty. Suppose $1 \leq m = |G| < n$ and $\sum_v t_v^2 \leq T_2^2$. Then its expected query count is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-expectation}
 O\left(\frac{T_2}{\sqrt{m}}\left(1 + \ln \frac{n}{m}\right)\right),
\end{equation}
and an absolute constant $C \geq 1$ satisfies, for every $v \in G$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-distribution}
 \Pr[\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2) = v] \leq \frac{C}{m}.
\end{equation}
The probability that $\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2)$ returns $\bot$ is at most $\delta_m$, where the numbers $\delta_m$ depend only on $m$ and satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:false-emptiness}
 \sum_{m \geq 1} \delta_m < \frac{1}{100}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

We next use \eqref{eq:search-distribution} to bound the number and sizes of the candidate sets. Starting from $W_0 = \emptyset$ and $U_0 = [n]$, consider a process that at each reached step with $U_h = U(W_h) \neq \emptyset$ may stop or select a vertex of $U_h$ and append it to $W_h$. Given the preceding choices, each vertex has selection probability at most $C / |U_h|$. The process stops when the candidate set is empty, and all sets after stopping are empty. Put $m_h = |U_h|$, let $R = |\{h : m_h > 0\}|$, and let $W_{\mathrm{end}}$ be the final list.

For every $b \geq 0$, there are $O(b)$ vertices whose selection decreases the number of candidates by at most $b$. Together with the bound $C / |U_h|$ on each selection probability, this gives an expected decrease $\Omega(|U_h|)$, which underlies the first two estimates below. The full definition and proof are given in \Cref{app:candidate-estimates}.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:candidate-estimates}
For the candidate selections described above, starting from $U_0 = [n]$, the following estimates hold:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:completion-profile}
 \mathbb E R = O(\ln n), \quad \mathbb E \sum_{h:m_h > 0} m_h^{-1 / 2} = O(1), \quad \mathbb E \sum_{v = 1}^n t_v(W_{\mathrm{end}})^2 = O(n \ln^2 n).
\end{equation}
The first two estimates follow from the assumptions on the candidate selections. The third additionally assumes \eqref{eq:edge-square-sum}.
\end{lemma}

The first two estimates bound the expected query counts for classifications and repeated searches; the last estimate in \eqref{eq:completion-profile} justifies the choice of $T_2$ below.

\subsection{Finding a source}\label{subsec:source-algorithm}

Appending a vertex from $U(W)$ decreases the number of candidates and can increase the query counts $t_v(W)$. The bound on $\mathbb E \sum_v t_v(W_{\mathrm{end}})^2$ determines the parameter $T_2$ for each search, while the bounds on the number and sizes of the candidate sets control the total query count.

Choose sufficiently large absolute constants $K_2,K_T$ and put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:source-parameters}
 T_2 = \left\lceil K_2 \sqrt{n} \ln n\right\rceil, \qquad
 T_{\max} = \lceil K_T T_2 \ln n\rceil.
\end{equation}
The procedure $\mathrm{FindSource}$ first chooses the table of random positions described above. With this table fixed, it starts with a uniformly chosen vertex, sets $W$ to the list containing it, and stores its classification. While $|W| < n$, it runs $\mathrm{Search}(U(W),T_2)$. If the search returns $\bot$, the procedure returns the last vertex of $W$; if it returns an index outside $[n] \setminus W$, the procedure returns $1$. Otherwise it appends and classifies the returned vertex. When $|W| = n$, it returns the last vertex. Before a classification or membership circuit or its inverse would make the total query count exceed $T_{\max}$, including within a search, the procedure returns $1$. For this stopping rule, the circuit that computes a classification and its inverse each use $s_n$ queries, while $\widetilde{\mathcal M}_q$ and its inverse each use $2 q$.

The searches in $\mathrm{FindSource}$ use $\widetilde{\mathcal M}_q$ and its inverse. We first analyze the procedure obtained by replacing these circuits with $\mathcal M_q$ and its inverse. \Cref{lem:source-implementation} bounds the resulting change in output probabilities.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:source-implementation}
For every input and fixed table of positions, each output probability differs by $o(1)$ between the procedure using $\mathcal M_q$ and its inverse and the procedure using $\widetilde{\mathcal M}_q$ and its inverse, uniformly over the input and table. The unitary circuit for $\mathrm{FindSource}$ makes exactly $T_{\max}$ queries on every input. Measuring its output register gives the output distribution of $\mathrm{FindSource}$, and reversing its gates gives the inverse circuit.
\end{lemma}

The proof of \Cref{lem:source-implementation} and the pseudocode for $\mathrm{FindSource}$ are given in \Cref{app:source-implementation}. We can now prove \Cref{lem:block-finding}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{lem:block-finding}]
Fix $x$ satisfying $(i,S)$ and first fix a table for which the classification test succeeds. Then $i$ is the source of $\mathcal G$ and \eqref{eq:edge-square-sum} holds. Analyze $\mathrm{FindSource}$ using $\mathcal M_q$ without the stopping rule at $T_{\max}$. For the analysis only, the run halts after a vertex is appended and classified if $\sum_v t_v(W)^2 > T_2^2$, including after the initial choice. Let $W_{\mathrm{end}}$ be the final list, including any vertex whose append caused this stop, and let $T'$ be the total query count of this run.

The additional stopping rule is tested only between calls to $\mathrm{Search}$. Each call uses a list $W$ satisfying $\sum_v t_v(W)^2 \leq T_2^2$ and is executed until it returns an output. Fix the outcomes preceding a call. If $U(W) \neq \emptyset$, \Cref{lem:full-search} bounds the probability of returning each fixed vertex in $U(W)$ by $C / |U(W)|$. The initial choice is uniform, and a search on an empty set returns $\bot$ with certainty. Thus \Cref{lem:candidate-estimates} applies to the sequence of selections, including the last appended vertex: its selection obeys the same probability bound, and \eqref{eq:membership-completion-update} bounds the resulting increases in $t_v(W)$.

For the final list of selected vertices $W_{\mathrm{end}}$, the value $t_v(W_{\mathrm{end}})$ is the query count of the membership test for $v$ with correct comparison answers. By \eqref{eq:membership-completion-update}, $t_v(W) \leq t_v(W_{\mathrm{end}})$ at every earlier step. Markov's inequality and the last estimate in \eqref{eq:completion-profile} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:completion-profile-tail}
 \Pr\left[\sum_{v = 1}^n t_v(W_{\mathrm{end}})^2 > T_2^2\right] \leq \frac{1}{100}
\end{equation}
for sufficiently large $K_2$. After the initial choice, the positive sizes of the candidate sets are distinct and less than $n$. Suppose the outcomes preceding a search with $m > 0$ candidates are fixed. The probability that this search returns $\bot$ is then at most $\delta_m$. A union bound and \eqref{eq:false-emptiness} therefore bound the probability that any search returns $\bot$ on a nonempty candidate set by $1 / 100$.

For the query count, recall that $U_h = U(W_h)$ is the candidate set at step $h$ of the analyzed run and $m_h = |U_h|$. For each search with $m_h > 0$, \eqref{eq:search-expectation} bounds the expected query count, with the earlier outcomes fixed, by $O(T_2 \ln n / \sqrt{m_h})$. There is at most one search on an empty set, using $O(T_2 \ln n)$ queries. At most $R$ vertices are classified, each using $s_n = O(\ln n)$ queries. Applying the first two estimates in \Cref{lem:candidate-estimates} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:completed-search-query-count}
 \mathbb E T' = O\left(s_n \mathbb E R + T_2 \ln n\left(1 + \mathbb E \sum_{h:m_h > 0} m_h^{-1 / 2}\right)\right) = O(T_2 \ln n).
\end{equation}
Markov's inequality gives $\Pr[T' > T_{\max}] \leq 1 / 100$ for sufficiently large $K_T$.

Compare the run of $\mathrm{FindSource}$ using $\mathcal M_q$ and enforcing the maximum query count $T_{\max}$ with the analyzed run, using the same initial vertex and measurement outcomes whenever both runs execute the same circuit. Before the analyzed run reaches its additional stopping rule, a first difference can occur only if the run enforcing $T_{\max}$ returns $1$ before a circuit would make its query count exceed $T_{\max}$. The analyzed run completes that circuit, implying $T' > T_{\max}$. With probability at least $24 / 25$, neither stopping rule is reached and every search on a nonempty set returns a vertex. On this event the runs agree.

The source remains a candidate until selected, and each selection strictly decreases the candidate set by \eqref{eq:candidate-update}. Thus the source is eventually appended. It is then the last entry of the list and the candidate set is empty, so the procedure returns it.

By \Cref{lem:source-implementation}, for every table on which the classification test succeeds, $\mathrm{FindSource}$ returns $i$ with probability at least $24 / 25 - o(1)$. Together with the $11 / 12$ probability that the classification test succeeds, this gives total success probability at least $5 / 6$ for sufficiently large $n$. The same lemma gives fixed query count $T_{\max} = O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$ on every input.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Algorithms for \texorpdfstring{$H$ and $F_n$}{H and F\_n}}

The algorithm for $H$ runs $\mathrm{FindSource}$ and then searches the returned block $i$, with error at most $1 / 100$, for a position $p$ with $x_i(p) \wedge y_i(p) = 1$. It checks a reported position and returns one only if the check succeeds; otherwise it returns zero.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:query-upper}
The algorithm for $H$ has error at most $1 / 4$ on its domain and maximum query count $O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$ on every input. It has a unitary implementation with fixed query count $T_H = O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$. Measuring the circuit's output register gives the algorithm's output distribution, and reversing its gates gives the inverse circuit.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $x$ satisfies $(i,S)$. By \Cref{lem:block-finding}, $\mathrm{FindSource}$ returns $i$ with probability at least $5 / 6$. For this block, $x_i(p) \wedge y_i(p) = 1$ if and only if $p \in S$ and $y_i(p) = 1$.

The search in the returned block uses $O(\sqrt{n})$ queries by \cite[Theorem~3]{BuhrmanCleveDeWolfZalka}. Each query to the string $(x_i(p) \wedge y_i(p))_{p \in [n]}$ is implemented with four queries to $(x,y)$: the circuit queries $x_i(p)$ and $y_i(p)$, adds their conjunction to the response bit, and uncomputes the two queried bits while leaving the register containing $i$ unchanged. Hence the algorithm for $H$ has error at most $1 / 6 + 1 / 100 < 1 / 4$ and maximum query count $O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$.

By \Cref{lem:block-finding}, the circuit for $\mathrm{FindSource}$ stores the returned block index in its output register. This register controls the subsequent search without being measured. The search has fixed query count $O(\sqrt{n})$ and stores its outcomes as in \Cref{app:implementations}. The resulting circuit has fixed query count $T_H = O(\sqrt{n} \ln^2 n)$ on every input and the stated output distribution.
\end{proof}

The algorithm for $F_n$ recovers an address using this circuit for $H$, checks that cell, and returns its acceptance bit. By \Cref{lem:query-transfer} and $r = \Theta(\ln n)$,
\[
 \operatorname{Q}(F_n) = O\left(r T_H + \sqrt{n r} \ln n\right) = O(\sqrt{n} \ln^3 n).
\]

\section{Variable-time search}\label{app:variable-search}

\subsection{Search with a fixed number of stages}\label{subsec:variable-search}

For $G \subseteq [n]$, we first construct searches with fixed stage parameters and then combine them into $\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2)$ to prove \Cref{lem:full-search}.

Consider a checking family $\mathcal M_q$, indexed by integers $q \geq 0$, in the model of \cite[Section~2]{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs}. For each $v \in [n]$, let the stopping query count $t_v \geq 1$ be the first value of $q$ at which $\mathcal M_q$ reports whether $v \in G$ rather than $*$. These counts are fixed for the given input but need not be known to the search procedure. Encode the answers $*,0,1$ as $00,01,10$, respectively. Define the action of $\mathcal M_q$ by
\[
 \mathcal M_q \ket{v,z} =
 \begin{cases}
  \ket{v,z}, & q < t_v,\\
  \ket{v,z \oplus 10}, & q \geq t_v \text{ and } v \in G,\\
  \ket{v,z \oplus 01}, & q \geq t_v \text{ and } v \notin G,
 \end{cases}
\]
where $v \in [n]$ and $z \in \{0,1\}^2$. In this appendix, each application of $\mathcal M_q$ or its inverse is counted as $2 q$ queries, matching the query count of $\widetilde{\mathcal M}_q$ or its inverse in \Cref{lem:membership-implementation}.

Let $T_2 \geq \sqrt{n}$ be a known parameter used as an upper bound on $\left(\sum_{v = 1}^n t_v^2\right)^{1 / 2}$  below.  Put $q_0 = \lceil 3 T_2 / \sqrt{n} \rceil$, $J = \lceil \log_9 n \rceil$, and $q_j = 3^j q_0$ for $1 \leq j \leq J$.  Then $9 T_2^2 \leq n q_0^2 \leq 16 T_2^2$ and $q_J < 12 T_2$. For $h \in [J]$, call an index $v$ \emph{resolved at stage $h$} when $t_v \leq q_h$. The answer produced by $\mathcal M_{q_j}$ is updated by applying $\mathcal M_{q_j}$ again, returning the answer register to $00$, and then applying $\mathcal M_{q_{j + 1}}$. These applications use $2(q_j + q_{j + 1}) \leq 4 q_{j + 1}$ queries, and the inverse applies them in reverse order.

At each stage, amplitude amplification is applied to indices already identified as members of $G$ and to indices whose checks remain unresolved. The latter are included because a check at a later stage may identify them as members of $G$.

We use the recursive construction of \cite[Algorithm~1]{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs}, including the check at the end of each stage as in the proof of its Lemma~1. The response register of $\mathcal M_q$ is the answer register of the search. Put
\[
 \mathcal H_{\mathrm{search}} = \mathcal H_{\mathrm{vertex}} \otimes \mathcal H_{\mathrm{response}}, \qquad
 \Pi = I_{\mathrm{vertex}} \otimes \left(\ket{00} \bra{00} + \ket{10} \bra{10}\right).
\]
Let $\ket{0}_{\mathrm{search}}$ be the all-zero basis state of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{search}}$. The circuits $\mathcal A_j$ act on this space. The circuit $\mathcal A_1$ prepares the uniform vertex state and applies $\mathcal M_{q_1}$. For $1 \leq j < J$, one amplitude amplification step is followed by replacing the answer of $\mathcal M_{q_j}$ with that of $\mathcal M_{q_{j + 1}}$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-recursion}
 \mathcal A_{j + 1} = \mathcal M_{q_{j + 1}} \mathcal M_{q_j}
 \mathcal A_j (2 \ket{0}_{\mathrm{search}} \bra{0}_{\mathrm{search}} - I_{\mathrm{search}}) \mathcal A_j^\dagger
 (I_{\mathrm{search}} - 2 \Pi) \mathcal A_j.
\end{equation}
For $h \in [J]$, the procedure $\mathcal B_h$ runs $\mathcal A_h$ independently $200$ times and returns the first index whose answer is one, or $\bot$ if no execution has answer one. Put $\rho = 1 / 1000$. If one execution of $\mathcal A_h$ yields an index whose answer is one with probability at least $1 / 25$, then independence of the $200$ executions gives $\Pr[\mathcal B_h = \bot] \leq (24 / 25)^{200} < \rho$.
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:search-stage}
For each $h \in [J]$, $\mathcal B_h$ returns an index in $G$ or $\bot$, with maximum query count $O(h q_h)$. The probabilities $\Pr[\mathcal B_h = v]$ are equal over the members of $G$ resolved at stage $h$ and are zero for every other index. For each $v \in G$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-stage-point-mass}
 \Pr[\mathcal B_h = v] \leq 200 \frac{9^{h - 1}}{n}.
\end{equation}
If $1 \leq m = |G| < n$ and $\sum_v t_v^2 \leq T_2^2$, then, for $\ell = \lceil\log_9(n / m)\rceil$, at least $8 m / 9$ members of $G$ are resolved at stage $\ell$ and $\Pr[\mathcal B_\ell = \bot] \leq \rho$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The checking circuits return answer one only for members of $G$, and $\mathcal B_h$ returns only an index with that answer. We bound the amplitudes and query counts for all stages, then identify a stage with constant success probability.

We track the indices in $G$ together with those whose checks remain unresolved, since an unresolved check may still return one. Let $G_j = G \cup \{v : t_v > q_j\}$. We prove by induction that a real scalar $\alpha_j$ gives the common amplitude of these indices:
\[
 \Pi \mathcal A_j \ket{0}_{\mathrm{search}} = \alpha_j \left(\sum_{\substack{v \in G\\t_v \leq q_j}} \ket{v} \ket{10} + \sum_{\substack{v \in [n]\\t_v > q_j}} \ket{v} \ket{00}\right).
\]
The two sums contain one term for every $v \in G_j$, each with amplitude $\alpha_j$. Their total probability is $p_j = \|\Pi \mathcal A_j \ket{0}_{\mathrm{search}}\|^2 = |G_j|\alpha_j^2$.

For $j = 1$, the uniform initial state gives
$\alpha_1 = 1 / \sqrt{n}$. Suppose this identity holds at stage $j$. Applied to $\mathcal A_j \ket{0}_{\mathrm{search}}$, one amplification step multiplies each component in the range of $\Pi$ by $3 - 4 p_j$. The subsequent applications of $\mathcal M_{q_j}$ and
$\mathcal M_{q_{j + 1}}$ change the answer encoding without changing
the amplitude associated with an index; after these applications,
the components in the range of $\Pi$ are those indexed by
$G_{j + 1}$. The calculation in
\cite[Lemma~2]{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-stage-amplitude}
 \alpha_{j + 1} = \alpha_j (3 - 4 p_j),
 \qquad |\alpha_j| \leq \frac{3^{j - 1}}{\sqrt{n}}.
\end{equation}
The second bound follows by induction from $0 \leq p_j \leq 1$ and
$|3 - 4 p_j| \leq 3$.

At the output of $\mathcal A_h$, every member of $G$ resolved at stage $h$ has amplitude $\alpha_h$, so these members have equal return probabilities. Since the $200$ independent executions use separate registers, the distribution of the next execution is unchanged when none of the earlier executions has answer one; hence $\mathcal B_h$ returns each resolved member with the same probability. For a fixed $v \in G$, one execution returns $v$ with probability at most $|\alpha_h|^2 \leq 9^{h - 1} / n$. A union bound over the executions gives \eqref{eq:search-stage-point-mass}.

We prove by induction that $\mathcal A_j$ and its inverse use at most $4 j q_j$ queries. This holds for $j = 1$, since $\mathcal A_1$ uses $2 q_1$ queries. If it holds at stage $j$, then \eqref{eq:search-recursion} uses at most $12 j q_j + 2(q_j + q_{j + 1}) \leq 4(j + 1)q_{j + 1}$ queries, because $q_{j + 1} = 3 q_j$. Since $\mathcal B_h$ runs $\mathcal A_h$ $200$ times, it uses $O(h q_h) = O(h 3^h q_0)$ queries.

Assume now that $1 \leq m < n$ and $\sum_v t_v^2 \leq T_2^2$.
Set $\ell = \lceil \log_9(n / m) \rceil$. Iterating \eqref{eq:search-stage-amplitude} gives $\alpha_\ell = 3^{\ell - 1} n^{-1 / 2} \prod_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1}(1 - 4 p_j / 3)$. To bound $\alpha_\ell$ from below, it suffices to prove $\sum_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1} p_j \leq 1 / 4$. Since
$p_j = |G_j|\alpha_j^2$,
$|G_j| \leq m + |\{v \in [n] : t_v > q_j\}|$, and
$|\alpha_j|^2 \leq 9^{j - 1} / n$, summing over
$j = 1,\ldots,\ell - 1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-projection-sum}
 \sum_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1} p_j
 \leq \frac{m}{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1} 9^{j - 1}
 + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{v = 1}^n
 \sum_{\substack{1 \leq j < \ell\\q_j < t_v}} 9^{j - 1}.
\end{equation}
The definition of $\ell$ gives $9^{\ell - 1} < n / m$, so the first term on the RHS of \eqref{eq:search-projection-sum} is less than $1 / 8$. For a fixed $v$, extend the inner sum to all $j \geq 1$ satisfying $3^j q_0 < t_v$. The resulting geometric sum is less than $t_v^2 / (8 q_0^2)$. Hence the second term on the RHS of \eqref{eq:search-projection-sum} is at most
$\frac{1}{8 n q_0^2} \sum_{v = 1}^n t_v^2 \leq 1 / 8$.

Thus $\sum_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1} p_j \leq 1 / 4$. In particular,
$0 \leq 4 p_j / 3 \leq 1 / 3$ for every $j < \ell$, and
\[
 \prod_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1}
 \left(1 - \frac{4 p_j}{3}\right)
 \geq 1 - \frac{4}{3} \sum_{j = 1}^{\ell - 1} p_j
 \geq \frac{2}{3}.
\]
The resulting lower bound on the product gives
$\alpha_\ell \geq (2 / 3)3^{\ell - 1} / \sqrt{n}$.

The definitions of $q_0$ and $\ell$ give $n q_0^2 \geq 9 T_2^2$ and $9^\ell \geq n / m$. Hence $q_\ell^2 = 9^\ell q_0^2 \geq 9 T_2^2 / m$, and
\[
 \left|\{v \in G : t_v > q_\ell\}\right|
 < \frac{T_2^2}{q_\ell^2}
 \leq \frac{m}{9},
\]
so at least $8 m / 9$ members of $G$ are resolved at stage $\ell$.
One execution of $\mathcal A_\ell$ therefore has answer one at an index in $G$ with probability at least $(8 m / 9)\alpha_\ell^2$. Since $9^{\ell - 1} \geq n / (9 m)$, the lower bound on $\alpha_\ell$ gives
$\frac{8 m}{9}\alpha_\ell^2 \geq \frac{32}{729} > \frac{1}{25}$. Thus $\Pr[\mathcal B_\ell = \bot] \leq \rho$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Search with an unknown number of solutions}\label{subsec:complete-search}\label{app:search-circuit}

Define $\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2)$ by the following procedure. Its output lies in $[n] \cup \{\bot\}$. For $1 \leq m = |G| < n$ with $\sum_v t_v^2 \leq T_2^2$, \Cref{lem:search-stage} shows that the procedure $\mathcal B_\ell$, where $\ell = \left\lceil \log_9(n / m) \right\rceil$, returns a member of $G$ with probability at least $1 - \rho$. Since $m$ is unknown, the procedure cannot select $\mathcal B_\ell$ in advance. Following \cite[Algorithm~2]{AmbainisKokainisVihrovs}, round $j$ runs $\mathcal B_1,\ldots,\mathcal B_j$. Each call to $\mathcal B_h$ initializes fresh index, answer, and work registers to zero for its $200$ executions of $\mathcal A_h$. Once $j \geq \ell$, every subsequent round therefore includes a fresh application of $\mathcal B_\ell$.

\begin{algorithm}[H]
\caption{The procedure $\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2)$}
\label{alg:complete-search}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Procedure{$\mathrm{Search}$}{$G,T_2$}
  \For{$j = 1,\ldots,J$}
    \For{$h = 1,\ldots,j$}
      \State $v \gets \mathcal B_h$
      \If{$v \neq \bot$}
        \State \Return $v$
      \EndIf
    \EndFor
  \EndFor
  \State \Return $\bot$
\EndProcedure
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

For a unitary implementation, each call to $\mathcal B_h$ uses separate index and answer registers for its $200$ applications of $\mathcal A_h$. An output register records the index from the first application whose answer register contains the encoding of $1$, or $\bot$ if no application has such an answer.

The calls to $\mathcal B_h$ follow the order specified by \Cref{alg:complete-search}. After each call, a new register copies the previously recorded value if it differs from $\bot$, and otherwise copies the current output. The registers holding these values remain unchanged. The next call to $\mathcal B_h$ is controlled on the new register containing $\bot$. Thus, once an index has been recorded, every remaining call acts as the identity on that subspace. Measuring the final register gives the same output distribution as \Cref{alg:complete-search}. The ranges $1 \leq h \leq j \leq J$, together with the $200$ applications of $\mathcal A_h$ in each $\mathcal B_h$, determine a fixed sequence of circuit applications. All intermediate registers remain part of the circuit, so reversing all gates gives the inverse circuit.

\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{lem:full-search}]
By \Cref{lem:search-stage}, every returned index belongs to $G$, so an empty set gives output $\bot$ with certainty. For every $\ell \in [J]$, the query count through round $\ell$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:double-sum-estimate}
 O\left(q_0 \sum_{j = 1}^\ell \sum_{h = 1}^j h 3^h\right) = O(\ell 3^\ell q_0).
\end{equation}
Taking $\ell = J$ and using $q_J < 12 T_2$ gives maximum query count $O(T_2 \ln n)$ for every $G$ and every choice of $t_v$.

Assume that $1 \leq m < n$ and $\sum_v t_v^2 \leq T_2^2$, and put $\ell = \lceil\log_9(n / m)\rceil$. By \Cref{lem:search-stage}, $\mathcal B_\ell$ returns an index with probability at least $1 - \rho$ whenever it is run on fresh registers. Round $j > \ell$ uses $O(j 3^j q_0)$ queries and is reached with probability at most $\rho^{j - \ell}$, since every preceding round from $\ell$ onward runs $\mathcal B_\ell$ on fresh registers. Thus the expected query count after round $\ell$ is
\[
 O\left(q_0 \sum_{j = \ell + 1}^J j 3^j \rho^{j - \ell}\right) = O(\ell 3^\ell q_0),
\]
because $3 \rho < 1$. Together with \eqref{eq:double-sum-estimate}, $3^\ell < 3 \sqrt{n / m}$, and $q_0 \leq 4 T_2 / \sqrt{n}$, this proves \eqref{eq:search-expectation}.

Each round $\ell,\ldots,J$ runs $\mathcal B_\ell$ on fresh registers. Since $J - \ell \geq \lfloor\log_9 m\rfloor$,
\[
 \Pr[\mathrm{Search}(G,T_2) = \bot] \leq \rho^{J - \ell + 1}
 \leq \rho^{1 + \lfloor\log_9 m\rfloor}.
\]
Taking $\delta_m = \rho^{1 + \lfloor\log_9 m\rfloor}$ gives \eqref{eq:false-emptiness}, since
\[
 \sum_{m \geq 1} \delta_m = \sum_{a \geq 0} 8 \cdot 9^a \rho^{a + 1} = \frac{8 \rho}{1 - 9 \rho} < \frac{1}{100}.
\]

Fix $v \in G$. For $h < \ell$, there are at most $\ell - h$ calls to $\mathcal B_h$ before round $\ell$, and the call in round $j \geq \ell$ is reached with probability at most $\rho^{j - \ell}$. The expected total number of calls to $\mathcal B_h$ is therefore at most $\ell - h + 1 / (1 - \rho)$. Every call starts in fresh registers, so the output distribution of a reached call is unaffected by the outputs of earlier calls. Hence \eqref{eq:search-stage-point-mass} bounds the probability that a reached call returns $v$. Thus the probability of returning $v$ in a call with $h < \ell$ is at most
\[
 \frac{200}{n} \sum_{h = 1}^{\ell - 1}
 \left(\ell - h + \frac{1}{1 - \rho}\right)9^{h - 1}
 = O\left(\frac{9^{\ell - 1}}{n}\right) = O(1 / m).
\]
The first bound follows by substituting $d = \ell - h$ and summing the convergent series $\sum_{d \geq 1}(d + 1 / (1 - \rho))9^{-d}$.

Since $q_h$ is nondecreasing in $h$, at least $8 m / 9$ members of $G$ are resolved at every stage $h \geq \ell$. The equal return probabilities in \Cref{lem:search-stage} therefore bound the probability of returning any fixed $v$, given that the call returns an index, by $9 / (8 m)$. The first call in this range that returns an index obeys the same bound. Combining the two ranges proves \eqref{eq:search-distribution} for an absolute constant $C$.
\end{proof}

In \eqref{eq:search-recursion}, $\mathcal A_{j + 1}$ contains three applications of $\mathcal A_j$ or its inverse and two further membership checking circuits. Since $\mathcal A_1$ contains one checking circuit, this recurrence gives $2 \cdot 3^{j - 1} - 1$ applications in $\mathcal A_j$ of membership checking circuits or their inverses. Including the $200$ applications of $\mathcal A_h$ in each $\mathcal B_h$, the number in one complete $\mathrm{Search}$ circuit is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:search-circuit-count}
 O\left(\sum_{j = 1}^J \sum_{h = 1}^j 3^h\right) = O(3^J) = O(\sqrt{n}).
\end{equation}

\section{Proofs for the source algorithm}\label{app:comparisons-membership}

The circuit for $\mathrm{FindSource}$ applies the circuits for comparing blocks and testing candidate membership in superposition over their index registers. The constructions below define their action on basis states and convert bounds on the probability of an incorrect answer into norm bounds for compositions of these circuits.

\subsection{Unitary implementations}\label{app:implementations}\label{app:answer-addition}

In each unitary implementation below, the circuit prepares every random choice in its own register and copies each intermediate computational basis outcome to a separate register instead of measuring it. Each possible return has a fresh register consisting of a flag and an output field, initialized to the all-zero state $\ket{\mathrm{init}}$. When that return occurs, the circuit sets the flag to one and writes the returned value in the output field. Suppose the procedure makes at most $T$ queries for every sequence of stored values. For each $t \in [T]$, input-independent gates controlled by those values advance the computation on each corresponding subspace to its $t$th query or to a return, and move the relevant address and response data to common query registers. A controlled application of the standard oracle, implemented with one query, performs the $t$th query on every subspace where no return has been recorded and acts as the identity on the remaining subspaces. After the $T$th oracle application, the remaining input-independent gates copy the output field of the first return register not in $\ket{\mathrm{init}}$ to a designated output register initialized to zero, leaving all return registers unchanged. Measuring this output register gives the procedure's output distribution, and reversing all gates gives the inverse circuit.

Fix an integer $m \geq 1$ and strings $a_j \in \{0,1\}^m$. Let $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{index}}$, $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{answer}}$, $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aux}}$, and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{response}}$ be the state spaces of the index, answer, auxiliary, and response registers, respectively. The answer and response registers contain $m$ qubits. Put $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{work}} = \mathcal H_{\mathrm{answer}} \otimes \mathcal H_{\mathrm{aux}}$. The joint state space is
\[
 \mathcal H_{\mathrm{index}} \otimes \mathcal H_{\mathrm{work}} \otimes \mathcal H_{\mathrm{response}}.
\]
Let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unitary-by-index}
 \mathcal U = \sum_j \ket{j} \bra{j} \otimes \mathcal U_j \otimes I_{\mathrm{response}},
\end{equation}
where each $\mathcal U_j$ is unitary on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{work}}$. Define $\mathcal C \ket{j,z} = \ket{j,z \oplus a_j}$ and extend it by the identity on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{work}}$.
